answer: Hypothesis: The prevalence of non-native plants introduced via the gardening pathway varies strongly by habitat type in the Barcelona province (habitat × pathway chi-square = 48.8, df = 9, p = 1.8e-07; permutation test on plot labels p = 0.0005). Overall, 35.1% of the non-native plant species recorded across 632 plots (169 of 481) were gardening-introduced, but the per-habitat gardening share is not uniform: it is highest in Wetlands (55.8%, 95% CI 42.3–68.4%) and Coastal habitats (53.5%, CI 38.9–67.5%), remains high in Riparian (36.5%, CI 27.5–46.4%) and Urban (29.8%, CI 23.1–37.5%) habitats, and is lowest in Croplands (18.5%, CI 12.3–26.9%), with Meadows (30.8%, CI 12.7–57.6%) and Scrublands (40.0%, CI 11.8–76.9%) intermediate but uncertain due to small totals. The gradient therefore runs from a dominant gardening share in low-elevation, human-adjacent habitats (Wetlands, Coastal, Riparian, Urban; mean elevation 176–386 m) to a minority share in agricultural land, where non-natives are dominated by other pathways. The same habitats are also the most likely to contain at least one gardening-introduced species per plot (Wetlands 50.0%, Urban 47.7%, Coastal 44.8%, Riparian 36.1%, versus 20.7% in Croplands and <8% in Meadows, Scrublands and forests). In forest habitats and Rock outcrops gardening-introduced species are near-absent, but this rests on only 4–8 total non-native species and is reported as a caveat rather than a finding. The pattern sits against a recent regional shift — gardening accounts for 75.2% of species introductions recorded in 1985–2019 versus 16.8% before 1500 — and is consistent with the species-level record, in which 42 of 81 invaded species are gardening-introduced. Phylogenetic structure was inspected but is not relevant to this habitat-by-pathway prevalence question.

payload.hypothesis: Gardening-introduced non-native plants are disproportionately prevalent in low-elevation, human-adjacent habitats (Wetlands 55.8%, Coastal 53.5%, Riparian 36.5%, Urban 29.8% of recorded non-natives) and least prevalent in Croplands (18.5%), against an overall 35.1% gardening share; habitat variation is highly significant (chi2=48.8, df=9, p=1.8e-07; permutation p=0.0005). Forest and Rock outcrop habitats show near-absent gardening share but on 4-8 total species (caveat only). Context: gardening rose to 75.2% of introductions in 1985-2019 vs 16.8% before 1500.
payload.workflow: 1) Loaded and validated invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots, tab-separated, 0 NAs, no duplicate rows/coordinates; n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo == n.total in all 632 rows; one mutually exclusive habitat label per plot, 10 levels). 2) Built the per-habitat table: plot count, sum n.gard, sum n.total, gardening share with Wilson 95% CIs, and % of plots with >=1 gardening species. 3) Primary test: chi-square of independence on the aggregated habitat x {Gardening, other} species-count table (chi2=48.8, df=9, p=1.79e-07); per-habitat contributions to chi2 reported. 4) Robustness: plot-level permutation test (1999 shuffles of habitat labels among the 191 plots with n.total>0) giving p=0.0005; the unpenalized binomial GLM (n.gard ~ habitat, n.total as trials) diverges due to quasi-complete separation in the tiny forest cells (Broad-leaved 3/3 positive plots 100% gardening; Coniferous 4/5), noted and not pursued per guardrail. 5) Context only, no covariate adjustment (collinear with habitat): temporal contingency table (Gardening share 16.8% -> 75.2% across four periods), species-level cross-check (42/81 gardening-introduced), mean elevation by habitat. Phylogenetic tree inspected (76 tips, 75/81 species mapped) and deemed irrelevant to this question. Executed with python3/pandas/scipy; full output in analysis/output.txt.
